analysis.one_liner: Adds a 7% tax on corporate profits reported to shareholders over $100 million.
analysis.headline: The bill sat in the Senate Finance Committee from August 2021 until the end of the 117th Congress in January 2023 and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put an extra 7% tax on the profits big corporations report on their financial statements (their 'book income') above $100 million. Companies that already pay large amounts of regular corporate tax would get a credit that lowers the surtax, so the tax falls hardest on companies that report huge profits to shareholders but pay little federal income tax — often because of deductions, credits, and offshore arrangements. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, in two ways: the revenue raised from highly profitable corporations reduces how much the rest of the tax code has to raise, and the bill is aimed at the gap between the profits corporations report to shareholders and the taxable income they report to the IRS. Companies that already pay tax near the top corporate rate pay little or nothing extra.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an additional 7% tax on a corporation's adjusted net book income — the profit it reports on its financial statements — for the portion above $100 million a year [S3].
Because the tax is based on financial-statement income rather than taxable income, it reaches companies whose shareholder-reported profits exceed what they report to the IRS [S3].
Allows a credit equal to 33% of a company's net regular tax liability above the top corporate rate applied to $100 million, so firms already paying substantial regular tax pay a reduced surtax [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large corporations with more than $100 million in annual financial-statement income, especially those that report big profits to shareholders while paying low federal income tax; shareholders through lower returns and potentially some consumers through prices.

drawbacks.text: Companies would pay tax on income measured by financial-statement rules rather than the tax code, a different standard than the rest of corporate taxation, which can create mismatches and compliance complexity [S3].

The credit for income taxes paid softens but does not eliminate double taxation: a corporation that fully pays regular corporate tax on the same income would still owe a reduced portion of the 7% surtax [S3].

A new tax on reported profits gives companies a reason to restructure how they report income, and costs of a corporate tax can be partially passed through to shareholders, workers, or consumers over time [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core design is targeted: the credit means the surtax bites hardest where the gap between shareholder-reported profits and taxes paid is largest, which is the stated point. The tradeoffs are real but manageable — dual measurement standards add complexity, and some pass-through of costs is possible — but the bill was never seriously considered, so no weighing of a final version occurred.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Elizabeth Warren introduced the bill on August 9, 2021 with four original cosponsors: Sens. Angus King (I-ME), Jeff Merkley (D-OR), Ed Markey (D-MA), and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) [S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action — no hearing, markup, floor vote, or House counterpart vote — appears in the action history for the remainder of the 117th Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large corporations with more than $100 million in reported profits, particularly those with large gaps between book income and taxable income, avoided a new 7% surtax because the bill never advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Big profitable corporations that pay little tax

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a 7% surtax on corporate book income above $100 million.

for.name: Sens. Angus King, Jeff Merkley, Ed Markey, and Sheldon Whitehouse

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on August 9, 2021 and held no hearing, markup, or vote on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats and the one independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republicans cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without action.

industries.industry: Large corporations with over $100 million in reported profits
industries.note: They would owe a new 7% surtax on book income above $100 million, with a credit that reduces the tax for companies already paying substantial regular corporate tax; the burden falls heaviest on firms reporting large shareholder profits while paying low taxes. Its death leaves current corporate tax treatment of book-versus-taxable income unchanged.

industries.industry: Corporate tax advisory and accounting firms
industries.note: A parallel tax on financial-statement income would have created new compliance and planning work; its failure keeps existing arrangements in place.
